symptoms: cramping pain in lower abdomen before or during periods
pain radiating to lower back and thighs
pain begins 1-2 days before period and lasts 2-3 days
guidance: Primary dysmenorrhea (no underlying disease) is very common and manageable. Apply a heating pad or hot water bottle to lower abdomen – it is as effective as painkillers. Ibuprofen or Mefenamic acid (if not contraindicated) taken at the start of period gives good relief. Light exercise like walking actually reduces cramps. If pain is severe enough to miss school or work, consult a doctor – it may be secondary dysmenorrhea due to endometriosis or fibroids.
precautions: Start pain relief medication at the very first sign of cramps – do not wait for pain to peak
Apply heat (hot water bottle, heated pad) to lower abdomen for 20 minutes
Avoid salty foods and caffeine in the days before period – they worsen cramps
Light yoga or walking during period helps reduce prostaglandin levels causing cramps
See a doctor if pain is not controlled by OTC medicines or is worsening over time

symptoms: cycle shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days
periods that vary significantly month to month
very light or very heavy flow when periods do come
may or may not have associated symptoms like acne or hair growth
guidance: Irregular periods are very common especially in the first 2 years after puberty and again approaching menopause. Common causes include stress, weight changes, thyroid problems, PCOS, and excessive exercise. Track your cycle for 3 months using a diary or app. Consult a doctor if irregularity persists beyond 3 months, if periods stop for more than 3 months, or if associated with other symptoms like weight gain, hair growth, or nipple discharge.
precautions: Track your menstrual cycle with dates for at least 3 months before doctor visit
Manage stress – it is one of the most common causes of irregular periods
Maintain a healthy weight – both underweight and overweight disrupt hormones
Do not self-medicate with hormonal pills without medical evaluation
Irregular periods in a sexually active person should prompt a pregnancy test first

symptoms: no menstruation by age 15-16 with breast development present
no menstruation by age 13-14 with no signs of puberty at all
no secondary sexual characteristics (no breast development, no pubic hair)
may have cyclical abdominal pain (if outflow obstruction)
guidance: Primary amenorrhea requires medical evaluation. Causes range from hormonal conditions, structural abnormalities, genetic conditions (Turner syndrome), to imperforate hymen (outflow obstruction). Do not dismiss it as 'late development' beyond age 15. Evaluation includes physical exam, hormone blood tests, and ultrasound. Most causes are treatable.
precautions: Consult a gynecologist if no periods by age 15 with breast development, or age 13 without any puberty signs
Do not delay evaluation – some structural causes worsen if untreated
Bring record of any other symptoms: headache, vision changes, weight changes
Cyclical lower abdominal pain without periods may indicate outflow blockage – needs urgent care
Do not start hormonal treatment without proper diagnosis

symptoms: previously regular periods stopping for 3 or more months
weight loss or excessive exercise history
guidance: First step: rule out pregnancy with a home pregnancy test. Other common causes include high stress, extreme weight loss or overexercise, PCOS, thyroid disorders, prolactin excess (pituitary adenoma), and premature ovarian insufficiency. Evaluation requires blood tests: pregnancy test, thyroid, prolactin, FSH, LH, AMH. Do not ignore amenorrhea – prolonged estrogen deficiency causes osteoporosis even in young women.
precautions: Always do a pregnancy test first before any other investigation
Do not over-exercise or restrict calories severely – athletic amenorrhea causes bone loss
Seek evaluation after 3 months of missed periods in a woman who previously had periods
Prolonged amenorrhea causes bone thinning – calcium and Vitamin D are essential
Do not self-prescribe progesterone pills to 'bring on' periods without diagnosis

symptoms: soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several consecutive hours
needing to use double protection (pad + tampon)
passing blood clots larger than a 50-paise coin
anemia symptoms: fatigue, dizziness, shortness of breath
needing to change pad at night
restricting activities due to heavy flow
guidance: Heavy periods are one of the most common causes of iron deficiency anemia in Indian women. Keep a period diary noting number of pads used per day. Causes include fibroids, endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, thyroid disorders, blood clotting problems, and hormonal imbalance. Treatment depends on cause: iron supplements for anemia, hormonal management, or surgery for structural causes. Do not accept heavy periods as 'just your fate.'
precautions: Start iron supplements immediately – heavy periods cause serious anemia
Track pad usage per day for your doctor visit (1 fully soaked pad = ~5-10 ml blood)
Avoid NSAIDs like aspirin as they can worsen bleeding
Ibuprofen or Mefenamic acid actually reduce heavy period bleeding – ask your doctor
Seek emergency care for soaking more than 1 pad per hour for 2+ consecutive hours

symptoms: acne on face, chest, or back
thinning scalp hair or male-pattern hair loss
darkened skin patches in skin folds (acanthosis nigricans)
multiple small cysts on ovaries on ultrasound
guidance: PCOS affects 1 in 5 Indian women and is the most common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age. It is a syndrome – not all women have all symptoms. Weight loss of even 5-10% of body weight significantly restores hormone balance and periods. Dietary changes (low glycemic index foods, less refined carbs) and regular exercise are first-line treatments. Medications include Metformin (improves insulin resistance), hormonal pills to regularize periods, and anti-androgens for hair and acne. PCOS increases lifelong risk of diabetes and heart disease.
precautions: Losing even 5-10% of body weight dramatically improves PCOS symptoms
Get screened for diabetes and prediabetes – PCOS causes insulin resistance
Do not rely on birth control pills alone long-term without addressing root cause
Exercise 30 minutes at least 5 days a week – proven to restore ovulation in PCOS
Annual screening for diabetes, cholesterol, and blood pressure is important in PCOS

symptoms: pain during or after sex (deep dyspareunia)
pain with bowel movements or urination during period
heavy periods or spotting between periods
pain may worsen progressively over years
guidance: Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 women but diagnosis takes an average of 7-10 years in India because symptoms are dismissed as 'normal period pain.' The tissue lining the uterus grows outside it – on ovaries, fallopian tubes, bowel, and bladder. It cannot be seen on ultrasound in early stages – diagnosis requires laparoscopy. Treatments: hormonal (birth control pills, GnRH agonists) or surgical. It does not always cause infertility but increases the risk.
precautions: Do not accept severe debilitating period pain as 'normal' – seek second opinion if needed
Track symptoms and severity with dates to show your gynecologist
Early diagnosis and treatment preserves fertility and prevents progression
Anti-inflammatory medications (ibuprofen, naproxen) help manage pain
Hormonal treatment suppresses the disease – do not stop without medical advice

symptoms: symptoms appear 5-10 days before period and disappear within 2-3 days of period starting
guidance: PMS is caused by hormonal fluctuations in the second half of the menstrual cycle and affects up to 75% of menstruating women to varying degrees. Lifestyle measures help significantly: reduce salt, sugar, and caffeine in the 2 weeks before period; exercise regularly; ensure adequate sleep; calcium supplements (1000mg/day) have strong evidence for reducing PMS symptoms. Severe PMS (PMDD) that impairs daily functioning should be evaluated by a doctor.
precautions: Track symptoms for 2-3 months to confirm the cyclic pattern (defines PMS)
Reduce salt and caffeine intake in the 2 weeks before period
Take calcium 1000mg daily – proven to reduce PMS mood and physical symptoms
Avoid alcohol in the premenstrual phase – it worsens mood symptoms
If symptoms are severe enough to impact work, relationships, or daily life – this is PMDD, seek medical help

symptoms: severe depression, hopelessness, or self-deprecating thoughts in the week before period
symptoms resolve within a few days of period starting and are absent the rest of the month
guidance: PMDD is a severe form of PMS that significantly impairs functioning and is classified as a depressive disorder – not 'just bad PMS.' It is caused by abnormal brain sensitivity to normal hormonal fluctuations. SSRIs (antidepressants) taken either throughout the cycle or only in the luteal phase are highly effective – 60-70% response rate. Hormonal treatments are also used. Seek psychiatric or gynecological evaluation – it is very treatable.
precautions: Track symptoms daily for 2 cycles with a mood diary – essential for diagnosis
PMDD is a real medical condition – do not dismiss it as 'being emotional'
SSRIs work faster for PMDD than for regular depression – sometimes relief in first cycle
Avoid alcohol, excess caffeine, and sleep deprivation in the luteal phase
Aerobic exercise and CBT have evidence for PMDD – use alongside medical treatment

symptoms: may cause no symptoms at all (incidental finding)
guidance: Fibroids are benign (non-cancerous) muscle tumors of the uterus affecting up to 40% of women over 40. Most cause no symptoms. Management depends on symptoms, size, location, and desire for future pregnancy. Options range from observation (small asymptomatic fibroids) to medication (to shrink or manage bleeding) to minimally invasive procedures (UAE – uterine artery embolization) to surgery (myomectomy preserves uterus, hysterectomy removes it). Fibroids do not become cancerous.
precautions: Do not panic – fibroids are almost always benign (non-cancerous)
Not all fibroids need treatment – many can be safely monitored
Maintain iron levels if bleeding is heavy – take iron supplements
Get follow-up ultrasound every 6-12 months to monitor size if not treated
Seek second opinion before agreeing to hysterectomy – many women can be managed with less invasive options

symptoms: dull aching lower abdominal pain on one side
sudden severe sharp pain (if cyst ruptures or twists – ovarian torsion)
nausea and vomiting with severe pain (torsion)
guidance: Most ovarian cysts are functional (develop as part of the normal cycle) and resolve on their own within 2-3 menstrual cycles without treatment. Ultrasound confirms diagnosis. Large cysts (over 5cm), persistent cysts, cysts in post-menopausal women, or those with concerning features need follow-up or surgical evaluation. Ovarian torsion (twisted ovary) is a surgical emergency – sudden severe one-sided pain with vomiting needs immediate hospital care.
precautions: Follow up with repeat ultrasound in 6-8 weeks for simple cysts – most resolve naturally
Seek EMERGENCY care for sudden severe one-sided lower abdominal pain with vomiting – may be torsion
Post-menopausal women with any ovarian cyst need prompt specialist evaluation
Do not Google your ultrasound report – ovarian cyst descriptions sound scarier than most are
PCOS cysts are different from simple ovarian cysts – they do not rupture or twist

symptoms: sudden severe one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain
pain may come in waves initially then become constant
abdomen is tender on one side
pain may radiate to back or thigh
guidance: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency where the ovary twists on its blood supply. If not operated within 4-6 hours, the ovary loses its blood supply and dies. Rush to hospital emergency immediately. Do not take painkillers and 'wait and see.' Doppler ultrasound helps diagnosis but a normal scan does NOT rule out torsion. Emergency laparoscopic surgery to untwist the ovary can save it if done quickly.
precautions: Seek EMERGENCY care immediately – do not wait for pain to subside
Do not take painkillers to manage at home – this masks a surgical emergency
A normal Doppler ultrasound does NOT rule out torsion – if pain persists, insist on surgical evaluation
Women with ovarian cysts or PCOS are at higher risk
Time to surgery directly determines whether the ovary can be saved

symptoms: light bleeding or spotting between regular periods
pink or brown discharge between periods
guidance: Causes range from benign (mid-cycle ovulation spotting, hormonal contraception side effects, implantation bleeding in early pregnancy) to serious (cervical polyps, cervical erosion, endometrial polyps, or rarely cervical or uterine cancer). Any bleeding after menopause must be evaluated urgently. Bleeding after sex should always be evaluated to rule out cervical pathology. Track when spotting occurs in relation to your cycle.
precautions: Any post-menopausal bleeding requires urgent gynecology evaluation – do not delay
Bleeding after sex should be evaluated to rule out cervical problems
Track exact timing in cycle – mid-cycle spotting at ovulation is often normal
Do a pregnancy test – implantation bleeding occurs around expected period time
Report to doctor if spotting occurs for more than 3 consecutive cycles

symptoms: NORMAL: clear to white, odorless or mild smell, increases around ovulation
BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS: grey-white watery discharge with strong fishy odor, worse after sex
YEAST INFECTION: thick white cottage-cheese-like discharge, intense itching and burning, no bad odor
TRICHOMONIASIS: yellow-green frothy discharge with foul smell, itching, redness
STI (chlamydia/gonorrhea): yellow or green discharge, may have pelvic pain or no symptoms
guidance: Normal vaginal discharge varies throughout the cycle – it is the vagina's self-cleaning mechanism. Do not douche – it destroys protective bacteria and worsens infections. Yeast infections are common after antibiotics and can be treated with antifungal cream or suppository (clotrimazole available OTC). Bacterial vaginosis and STIs require prescription antibiotics. STIs need partner treatment too. If in doubt – get examined rather than self-treating.
precautions: Do NOT douche – it disrupts the vaginal microbiome and promotes infections
Wear breathable cotton underwear and avoid tight synthetic clothing
Do not self-treat with antifungals more than once without diagnosis – recurring infections need evaluation
STIs often have no symptoms – get tested if you have a new or multiple partners
Complete the full antibiotic course for bacterial infections even if discharge resolves

symptoms: hot flashes (sudden intense heat, sweating, flushing)
vaginal dryness and discomfort during sex
mood changes: irritability, anxiety, low mood
urinary symptoms: urgency, frequency, recurrent UTIs
guidance: Menopause is a natural transition, not a disease, typically occurring between age 45-55 in Indian women. Perimenopause (transition phase) can last 2-10 years before periods stop. Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) is the most effective treatment for hot flashes and vaginal symptoms – discuss risks and benefits with doctor. Non-hormonal options: CBT for hot flashes, vaginal moisturizers for dryness, regular exercise for mood and bones. Calcium and Vitamin D are essential for bone health. This is a crucial time for cardiovascular and bone health monitoring.
precautions: Menopause before age 40 is Premature Ovarian Insufficiency – needs urgent medical evaluation
Any bleeding after 12 months of no periods must be evaluated for uterine cancer
Ensure adequate calcium (1200mg/day) and Vitamin D (600-800 IU/day) for bone protection
Get bone density (DEXA) scan at menopause especially with risk factors
Do not use herbal supplements claiming to 'balance hormones' without medical advice

symptoms: irregular or absent periods before age 40
hot flashes in a young woman
blood tests show high FSH and low estrogen
guidance: POI is not the same as early menopause – some women with POI can still ovulate intermittently and get pregnant. It requires urgent medical evaluation and treatment. Without estrogen replacement, young women with POI face high risk of osteoporosis, heart disease, and cognitive decline. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is recommended until average age of menopause (51 years). Causes include autoimmune conditions, genetic factors, and cancer treatment.
precautions: Start HRT early – unprotected estrogen deficiency at young age causes serious long-term harm
Pregnancy is still possible intermittently – use contraception if pregnancy not desired
Get bone density test and cardiovascular evaluation
Seek genetic counseling if POI is diagnosed under age 30
Psychological support is important – POI can cause grief and identity issues especially regarding fertility

symptoms: low blood pressure causing dizziness or fainting
sunburn-like red rash especially on palms and soles
redness of eyes, mouth, and throat
associated with prolonged tampon or menstrual cup use
guidance: TSS is a rare but life-threatening bacterial toxin emergency. Do NOT attempt home management – call 108 and go to hospital immediately. Remove tampon or menstrual cup immediately if wearing one. TSS requires IV antibiotics, IV fluids, and intensive care. Prevention: change tampons every 4-8 hours, use lowest absorbency needed, alternate with pads, and properly clean menstrual cups.
precautions: Change tampons every 4-8 hours – never leave overnight
Use lowest absorbency tampon for your flow on each day
Remove tampon immediately and go to emergency if fever develops while using one
Clean menstrual cups properly with boiling between cycles
Alternate tampon use with sanitary pads, especially overnight

symptoms: not a disease – preventive guidance for all menstruating individuals
guidance: Good menstrual hygiene prevents infections, rashes, and Reproductive Tract Infections (RTIs) which are very common in rural India. Change sanitary pads every 4-6 hours even with light flow. Wash hands before and after changing pad. Clean the genital area with plain water only – no soap inside the vagina. Dispose of pads properly (wrap and bin – do not flush). Menstrual cups and cloth pads are eco-friendly and cost-effective alternatives. Free pads are distributed under Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) at PHCs for adolescent girls.
precautions: Change pad every 4-6 hours even if flow is light – old blood breeds bacteria
Wash genital area with clean water only – no soap, no douching inside vagina
Wash hands before and after every pad change
Do not flush sanitary pads – wrap in paper and dispose in bin
Free sanitary pads available for adolescent girls at PHCs under RKSK program

symptoms: heavy painful periods that worsen over years
symptoms worsen with each cycle progressively
typically in women over 35 who have had children
guidance: Adenomyosis occurs when the endometrial tissue grows into the uterine muscle wall, causing it to enlarge and bleed internally during periods. It is often confused with fibroids but is a different condition. Diagnosis is by MRI or transvaginal ultrasound. Management: anti-inflammatory medicines, hormonal treatments (Mirena IUS is very effective), or hysterectomy in severe cases in women who have completed family. Adenomyosis resolves naturally after menopause.
precautions: Keep a pain and bleeding diary to monitor progression
Mirena IUS (hormonal coil) significantly reduces bleeding and pain – ask your doctor
Iron supplements are essential due to heavy blood loss
Hysterectomy is curative but should be last resort after other options tried
Symptoms improve dramatically after menopause – this information helps with management decisions

symptoms: often no symptoms – found on routine examination
guidance: Cervical polyps are benign (non-cancerous) finger-like growths on the cervix, common in women over 40 and those who have been pregnant. They are almost always benign but can cause abnormal bleeding. Removal is simple (done in clinic without anesthesia) and curative. The removed polyp should be sent for histology to confirm it is benign. Regular Pap smears and VIA screening help detect polyps along with cervical cancer.
precautions: Get a Pap smear or VIA test regularly – free at PHC/CHC
Report any bleeding after sex to a gynecologist
Polyp removal is a simple outpatient procedure – do not delay
All removed polyps should be sent for histopathology examination
Do not confuse cervical polyps with cervical cancer – they are almost always benign

symptoms: unusual vaginal discharge with bad odor
nausea and vomiting in severe cases
guidance: PID is an infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, usually caused by sexually transmitted bacteria (chlamydia, gonorrhea) or vaginal bacteria traveling upward. It must be treated promptly with antibiotics to prevent permanent damage to fallopian tubes causing infertility and ectopic pregnancy. Both partners must be treated for STI-related PID. Free treatment available at government hospitals. Tubo-ovarian abscess (severe PID with abscess) may need hospitalization.
precautions: Seek treatment early – delay causes scarring and infertility
Both sexual partners must be treated simultaneously
Complete the full antibiotic course even if pain improves
Avoid sex until both partners have completed treatment and symptoms resolved
IUD insertion in the setting of active STI can cause PID – get tested before IUD placement

symptoms: severe one-sided throbbing headache occurring 2 days before to 3 days after period starts
predictable cyclic pattern linked to menstrual cycle
guidance: Menstrual migraines are triggered by the drop in estrogen just before menstruation. They tend to be more severe and longer-lasting than non-menstrual migraines. Treatment: take prescribed migraine medication (triptan) at first sign of attack. Prevention: Frovatriptan taken 2 days before expected migraine can prevent it. NSAIDs (naproxen) started 2 days before period also help. Hormonal management to stabilize estrogen levels (continuous pill use) can eliminate menstrual migraines entirely.
precautions: Track migraine dates relative to period dates for 3 months to confirm menstrual trigger
Take triptan or NSAID at the very first sign of headache – do not wait
Ensure adequate sleep and hydration around period time
Avoid known migraine triggers in days before period: alcohol, stress, skipping meals
Discuss preventive medication options with neurologist or gynecologist

category: Period Poverty and Access to Menstrual Products
symptoms: using cloth, ash, sand, or unhygienic materials due to lack of access to sanitary products
missing school or work during periods
recurrent reproductive tract infections from unhygienic practices
guidance: Period poverty is a public health issue affecting millions of girls and women in India, leading to school dropout, RTIs, and long-term health impacts. Government programs: Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan, RKSK provide free or subsidized pads. Reusable cloth pads, when properly washed and dried in sunlight, are safe and cost-effective. Menstrual cups are highly cost-effective (one-time purchase lasting 10 years). ASHA workers and Anganwadi centers can connect to free pad distribution programs.
precautions: Cloth pads must be washed with soap, rinsed thoroughly, and dried in DIRECT SUNLIGHT
Never dry cloth pads indoors or in the dark – promotes bacterial growth
Menstrual cups are safe, reusable for 10 years, and available for under Rs. 300
Contact nearest Anganwadi or PHC for free sanitary pad access under RKSK
Talk openly with girls about menstrual hygiene – breaking stigma saves health

symptoms: mid-cycle lower abdominal pain (around day 14 of a 28-day cycle)
pain on one side, can be sharp or dull
may last a few minutes to a few hours
no fever or other signs of infection
guidance: Mittelschmerz is normal ovulation pain caused by the stretching of the ovarian capsule before the egg is released. It is harmless. For pain relief: heat packs and NSAIDs. If the pain is severe or lasts more than 2-3 days, rule out ovarian cyst or torsion.
precautions: Track cycle to identify if it is mid-cycle
Pain is typically mild – if severe, seek evaluation

symptoms: minimum pad usage (1-2 pads per day)
may be accompanied by brownish discharge
may indicate hormonal imbalance or uterine scarring
guidance: Light periods can be due to genetic variation, hormonal imbalance (low estrogen), excessive exercise, stress, or Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions). Evaluate if periods are suddenly lighter. Treat underlying cause: hormonal therapy, or hysteroscopy for adhesions.
precautions: If always light and regular, may be normal
Do not stop contraception if recently started – it may cause light periods
Monitor for pregnancy if light bleeding occurs

symptoms: may be regular but too frequent
guidance: Causes include uterine fibroids, polyps, endometriosis, or thyroid disorders. Evaluate with pelvic ultrasound and hormonal tests. Treatment addresses the underlying cause – hormonal therapy or surgical removal of pathology.
precautions: Check for anemia if bleeding is frequent
Do not ignore if causing iron deficiency

symptoms: heavy periods, frequent periods, or spotting between periods
not due to pregnancy or other organic causes
often due to anovulation (no egg release)
guidance: DUB is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out structural causes. Treatment: hormonal therapy (progestins, birth control pills) to regulate cycles. NSAIDs reduce bleeding. In severe cases, endometrial ablation or hysterectomy. Address underlying anovulation.
precautions: If bleeding is excessive, emergency care

symptoms: any vaginal bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea
may be pink, red, or brown
guidance: Postmenopausal bleeding is a warning sign for endometrial cancer. Urgent evaluation is required. Transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness, and endometrial biopsy if thickness > 4-5 mm. Other causes: atrophy, polyps, HRT. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not ignore any postmenopausal spotting
Endometrial biopsy is essential if thickened
Most cases are benign but early detection saves lives

guidance: Endometrial hyperplasia is a thickening of the uterine lining, often due to unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity, HRT). Without atypia – progestin therapy is effective (IUCD or oral). With atypia – risk of cancer; often hysterectomy. Regular follow-up with biopsy.

symptoms: heavy abnormal bleeding in premenopausal women
guidance: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer. It is highly curable if detected early. Treatment: hysterectomy, sometimes radiation/chemotherapy. Prevention: maintain healthy weight, manage diabetes, use progesterone with estrogen HRT. Early diagnosis saves lives.
precautions: Hysterectomy is curative in early stages

symptoms: early stages: often asymptomatic or vague
difficulty eating or feeling full quickly
guidance: Ovarian cancer is often diagnosed late (silent killer). Screening: transvaginal ultrasound and CA-125 in high-risk (BRCA, family history). Treatment: surgery and chemotherapy. Maintain healthy weight and lifestyle. BRCA testing and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy for carriers.

symptoms: burning, stinging, or rawness in the vulvar area
pain worse with sitting, sex, or tampon insertion
no visible infection or skin disease
guidance: Vulvodynia is poorly understood but real. Multidisciplinary: gynecology, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and pain management. Topical lidocaine, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin. Avoid irritants (soaps, tight clothing). CBT helps coping.

symptoms: involuntary contraction of pelvic muscles preventing vaginal penetration
pain with attempted intercourse, tampon insertion, or speculum exam
often associated with anxiety or trauma
guidance: Vaginismus is highly treatable. Pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal dilators (progressive use), CBT, and sex therapy. Address anxiety and build trust. Education and partner involvement. Success rate is high.

symptoms: pain localized to the vaginal opening (vestibule)
pain provoked by touch, sexual intercourse, or tampon insertion
guidance: A subtype of vulvodynia. Topical treatments (lidocaine, estrogen), physical therapy, and avoidance of irritants. Surgical vestibulectomy in refractory cases.

symptoms: white, wrinkled, thinned skin on vulvar area
guidance: Lichen sclerosus is an autoimmune inflammatory condition. Treatment: high-potency topical corticosteroids (clobetasol) is effective. Lifelong maintenance. In severe cases, surgery. Risk of vulvar cancer is increased – regular follow-up.
Vaginal estrogen therapy (creams, tablets, rings) is the gold standard. Systemic HRT also helps. Lubricants and moisturizers for symptom relief. Regular sexual activity improves blood flow.
precautions: Vaginal estrogen is safe and effective

symptoms: worse with standing, at end of day
may be associated with ovarian vein reflux
guidance: Diagnosed by ultrasound or MRI with venography. Treatment: lifestyle (avoid prolonged standing), pain management, hormonal therapy, or ovarian vein embolization (minimally invasive).

symptoms: often after dilation and curettage (D&C) or postpartum infections
guidance: Diagnosis by hysteroscopy. Treatment: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision. Followed by estrogen therapy to promote endometrial growth and prevent recurrence. Insertion of an intrauterine balloon or IUCD may help.

A septate uterus has a fibrous band dividing the uterine cavity. Diagnosis by MRI or 3D ultrasound. Hysteroscopic resection of septum (metroplasty) is performed in women with recurrent miscarriage or infertility.

symptoms: may cause recurrent miscarriage or preterm labor
guidance: Usually no treatment needed. If recurrent miscarriage, surgical unification (Strassman's procedure) is rarely done. Manage pregnancies as high-risk.

symptoms: no menstrual flow at puberty (primary amenorrhea)
guidance: Surgical incision of the hymen (hymenotomy) is curative. Drain the collected menstrual blood. It is a simple day procedure. If untreated, can cause infection and endometriosis.
Surgical resection of the septum. May be a transverse or longitudinal septum. Post-operative dilation to prevent stenosis.

symptoms: normal ovaries and secondary sexual characteristics
guidance: No surgical intervention for uterus (no pregnancy possible with own uterus). Vaginal dilators for functional vagina. Psychological support. Surrogacy or adoption options for family building.
precautions: Hormonal support (no estrogen needed as ovaries work)

category: Catamenial Epilepsy (Seizures Related to Menstrual Cycle)
symptoms: increase in seizure frequency around menstruation (peri-menstrual or mid-cycle)
seizures are more frequent during the perimenstrual phase when estrogen drops
guidance: Identify if seizures are catamenial. Hormonal therapy (progesterone) may help. Adjust anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) during the perimenstrual phase (clobazam, lorazepam). Neurosurgeon/neurologist consultation.
precautions: Track seizure calendar relative to cycle

symptoms: worsening of asthma symptoms in the premenstrual or perimenstrual phase
guidance: Adjust asthma medications before menstruation (controller therapy). NSAIDs (mefenamic acid) to reduce prostaglandins may help. Treat underlying allergic triggers. If severe, hormonal therapy.
precautions: NSAIDs for pain may help asthma

symptoms: galactorrhea (milk discharge from breasts not during breastfeeding)
guidance: Check prolactin levels. If elevated, do MRI pituitary. Treatment: dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) to lower prolactin and restore periods. If tumor is macroadenoma, surgery.

symptoms: milky nipple discharge not associated with breastfeeding
may be due to medications, stress, or prolactinoma
guidance: Stop offending drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics). If prolactin is high, treat with dopamine agonists. Reassurance if idiopathic. Rule out breast pathology.

category: Fibroadenoma (Benign Breast Lump) – Menstrual Hormone Influence
symptoms: smooth, firm, rubbery, mobile lump in breast
size may vary with menstrual cycle (hormone sensitive)
guidance: Fibroadenomas are benign. If asymptomatic, can be monitored. If growing or causing distress, remove (excision or cryoablation). Ultrasound is diagnostic. Reassurance.

symptoms: smooth, moveable, and may be tender
guidance: Ultrasound confirms simple cyst. Aspiration if painful or large. No cancer risk if simple. Fine-needle aspiration if complex. Reassurance.

category: Cyclic Mastalgia (Breast Pain with Menstrual Cycle)
symptoms: breast pain, heaviness, tenderness, swelling in the week before periods
guidance: Cyclical breast pain is normal and benign. Manage with: good support bra, avoid caffeine, evening primrose oil, and NSAIDs. If severe, hormonal therapy (danazol, tamoxifen) may be used.

symptoms: adnexal mass on ultrasound (classic 'ground glass' appearance)
ovarian endometriotic cyst filled with old blood
guidance: Endometriomas are associated with endometriosis. Surgical removal (cystectomy) is indicated if > 4 cm or causing pain/infertility. Hormonal suppression (GnRH agonists) may reduce recurrence. IVF may be needed.

Uterine sarcoma is aggressive. Treatment: hysterectomy, sometimes radiation and chemotherapy. A biopsy (endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy) is essential. Prognosis depends on stage. Prompt evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding.
Rare, associated with HPV. Treatment: radiation, surgery, or a combination. Routine pelvic exams and Pap smears can detect. HPV vaccine prevents vaginal cancer.

symptoms: lump, sore, or ulcer on vulva
changes in skin color (white, red, or dark)
may be associated with lichen sclerosus or HPV
guidance: Suspicious lesion needs biopsy. Treatment: surgery (wide local excision or vulvectomy), radiation. HPV vaccine prevents HPV-related vulvar cancer. Early detection is key.

symptoms: painful swelling at the vaginal opening (lower labia)
guidance: Small asymptomatic cyst: may resolve. Infected abscess: incision and drainage, or Word catheter placement for 4-6 weeks. Antibiotics (if cellulitis). Marsupialization for recurrent.
Vaginal estrogen cream (estradiol) is most effective. Systemic HRT also helps. Non-hormonal lubricants/moisturizers. Regular use of vaginal estrogen prevents UTIs and improves quality of life.
precautions: Monitor for endometrial hyperplasia (with systemic HRT)

symptoms: pain in pelvis or lower back
guidance: Pelvic floor physiotherapy (Kegel exercises, biofeedback) is first-line. Avoid constipation and heavy lifting. Pessary for support. Surgery if severe.

symptoms: sensation of something coming down from the vagina
guidance: Grade 1-2: physiotherapy (Kegels), ring pessary. Grade 3-4: surgery (hysterectomy or uterine suspension). Treat constipation and avoid straining.

symptoms: Cystocele: urinary frequency, urgency, incomplete voiding
Rectocele: constipation, sensation of bulging, need to splint vaginally to defecate
guidance: Pelvic floor physiotherapy. Pessary for support. Surgery (anterior/posterior repair) for significant symptoms. Avoid straining.

symptoms: leakage of urine with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exertion
may worsen during menstruation due to hormonal changes
guidance: Kegel exercises, pelvic floor physiotherapy, weight loss, and avoiding straining. Vaginal estrogen may help in postmenopausal women. Surgical: mid-urethral sling.
Bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron). Limit caffeine. Treat with behavioral therapy first.

category: Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (Menstrual Flare)
symptoms: chronic pelvic pain, pressure, or discomfort in the bladder
worse with bladder filling, relieved by voiding
guidance: Multidisciplinary: pain management, dietary modifications (avoid acidic foods), pelvic floor physiotherapy, and medications (amitriptyline, hydroxyzine). Bladder instillations (DMSO).
Diagnosed by elevated 17-OH progesterone. Treatment: corticosteroids (dexamethasone) to suppress adrenal androgens. Fertility treatment with ovulation induction. Genetic counseling.
precautions: Surgical correction of ambiguous genitalia if needed

symptoms: Hypothyroid: heavy periods (menorrhagia) or irregular periods, fatigue, cold intolerance
Hyperthyroid: light periods (hypomenorrhea) or amenorrhea, palpitations, weight loss
guidance: Screen with TSH. Treat hypothyroidism with levothyroxine (restores periods). Treat hyperthyroidism with antithyroid drugs (methimazole). Regular monitoring of thyroid function.
precautions: Hyperthyroid: avoid pregnancy during active disease

category: Diabetes Mellitus Effects on Menstrual Cycle
symptoms: may be associated with PCOS-like features
increased risk of UTIs and yeast infections
guidance: Tight glycemic control improves menstrual regularity. Manage diabetes with diet, exercise, and medications. If PCOS coexists, metformin may help. Regular gynecological checkups.
Weight loss (5-10% of body weight) significantly improves periods and ovulation. Diet and exercise are first-line. Treat associated conditions (PCOS, diabetes). Bariatric surgery in severe obesity.

Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation, weight restoration, and reduction of exercise. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for eating disorder. Estrogen replacement to protect bone health (HRT) until weight normalizes.
precautions: Do not ignore amenorrhea – causes osteoporosis

guidance: Reduce intensity, increase caloric intake (especially carbohydrates), and rest. Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation. HRT if bone density is affected. Educate on female athlete triad (disordered eating, amenorrhea, osteoporosis).

symptoms: often associated with high prolactin or thyroid disorders
guidance: Diagnosis: endometrial biopsy or progesterone level on day 21. Treatment: progesterone supplementation (vaginal or oral) in the luteal phase. Clomiphene citrate or hCG may be used to support ovulation.

symptoms: may have PCOS, thyroid, or stress as causes
guidance: Treat underlying cause. Ovulation induction with clomiphene or letrozole for fertility. Progestins to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Lifestyle changes.

symptoms: inability to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected sex (6 months if >35)
irregular periods, pelvic pain, previous STI history
guidance: Evaluation: ovulation assessment, semen analysis, ultrasound (ovarian reserve, tubal patency), and hysteroscopy/laparoscopy if needed. Free fertility services at some government hospitals under NHP. Treat underlying cause.
precautions: Male partner should also be evaluated
Don't delay – fertility declines with age
Consider lifestyle changes (stop smoking, reduce alcohol)

symptoms: excess terminal hair on face, chest, back, or abdomen
guidance: Evaluate for PCOS and CAH (17-OH progesterone). Treatment: weight loss, oral contraceptives, anti-androgens (spironolactone, finasteride), and cosmetic hair removal (laser, electrolysis).
precautions: Do not self-treat with unknown supplements

symptoms: acne worsening in the 7-10 days before periods
common in PCOS or women with high androgens
guidance: Treat with topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, or antibiotics. For severe flares, oral contraceptives or spironolactone. Avoid picking lesions. Use non-comedogenic skincare.

category: Catamenial Depression (Depression Flaring with Menstrual Cycle)
symptoms: worsening of depressive symptoms in the premenstrual phase
not meeting full PMDD criteria but significant
guidance: Antidepressants (SSRIs) can be taken continuously or just in the luteal phase (symptomatic treatment). CBT. Manage stress. Hormonal therapy (OCPs) may help.

category: Hormonal IUD (Mirena/Levonorgestrel) Side Effects – Menstrual Changes
symptoms: irregular bleeding or spotting in the first 3-6 months
guidance: Most side effects diminish after 3-6 months. If irregular bleeding is bothersome, NSAIDs may help. If amenorrhea is acceptable, it's normal. If persistent heavy bleeding after 6 months, rule out malposition.

symptoms: menstrual periods become heavier and longer
guidance: NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen) reduce blood loss by 20-50%. If bleeding is excessive or causing anemia, consider switching to hormonal IUD or other contraception. Always check for expulsion.
precautions: If heavy bleeding persists >6 months, consider removal

category: Breakthrough Bleeding on Combined Oral Contraceptives (OCPs)
symptoms: irregular spotting or bleeding while on active OCP pills
may indicate inconsistent pill-taking or malabsorption
guidance: Reassure most women; it often resolves. If persistent, try a different OCP (higher estrogen dose) or change progestin. Ensure consistent pill-taking (same time daily).
precautions: Take pill at the same time daily
Rule out pregnancy if missed pills

symptoms: no withdrawal bleeding during the placebo pills
guidance: If on continuous use, amenorrhea is normal. If on cyclic pills and no withdrawal bleed, do a pregnancy test (rule out pregnancy). If repeatedly negative, no concern.
precautions: Pregnancy test if no withdrawal bleed
No need for treatment if pregnancy ruled out
Consider if she wants withdrawal bleeding
Change to different pill if desired

symptoms: no periods for 3+ months after stopping OCPs
may be associated with underlying PCOS or hypothalamic amenorrhea
ovulation may take time to resume
guidance: Most women resume periods within 3 months. If no period, evaluate for PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, or thyroid. Induction of ovulation may be needed if fertility desired. Reassurance is key.

category: HRT (Hormone Replacement Therapy) – Effects on Bleeding
symptoms: cyclic or irregular bleeding on HRT
bleeding pattern depends on regimen (continuous vs. sequential)
breakthrough bleeding is common in first 6 months
guidance: If on sequential HRT, predictable withdrawal bleeding. If on continuous, may have irregular spotting. Any bleeding after 6 months of continuous HRT needs endometrial biopsy. Postmenopausal bleeding must be evaluated.

category: Breast Self-Examination (BSE) – Timing with Menstrual Cycle
symptoms: best performed 5-7 days after period ends (when breasts are least lumpy)
guidance: Teach BSE: look for changes, palpate all quadrants, axilla, and check for nipple discharge. If any lump or change, seek medical evaluation. Breast cancer screening: mammography for women >40.
precautions: Don't panic – most lumps are benign

category: VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) – Cervical Cancer Screening
symptoms: VIA is done for cervical cancer screening
guidance: VIA is done at PHCs and CHCs free of cost. If VIA positive, colposcopy and biopsy. HPV DNA testing is also available. Screening every 5 years for women 30-65. HPV vaccine for girls 9-14.

symptoms: not a disease – HPV DNA test for high-risk types (16, 18)
positive test indicates high risk for cervical cancer
guidance: HPV testing is done in women >30 years. If positive, triage with Pap or colposcopy. Most HPV infections clear spontaneously. Persistent high-risk HPV needs follow-up. HPV vaccine is preventive.
precautions: If HPV positive, do not panic – most clear

symptoms: not a disease – procedure to examine cervix, vagina, and vulva
guidance: Colposcopy is an outpatient procedure. Biopsy may cause mild cramping and spotting. Results in 1-2 weeks. If abnormal, LEEP or conization may be done. It is safe and accurate.
precautions: Post-procedure: avoid sex, tampons for 1 week

symptoms: not a disease – procedure to sample endometrium
for abnormal bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, or hyperplasia evaluation
guidance: Office procedure. Mild cramping and bleeding post-procedure. Results in a week. Used to diagnose endometrial cancer or hyperplasia. Essential for postmenopausal bleeding.
precautions: If heavy bleeding or fever, seek care

symptoms: not a disease – visualization of uterine cavity
for abnormal bleeding, polyps, fibroids, or retained products
guidance: Outpatient or day-care. Can be diagnostic or operative (remove polyps, fibroids, adhesions). Minimal recovery. Good for diagnosing Asherman's syndrome and septate uterus.
precautions: If fever or heavy bleeding, seek care
No sex or tampons for 1 week

category: Laparoscopy for Endometriosis Diagnosis and Treatment
symptoms: used to diagnose and treat endometriosis, ovarian cysts, adhesions
guidance: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for endometriosis diagnosis. Can also treat (excision or ablation). Recovery: 1-2 weeks. If pregnancy is desired, surgery can improve fertility. Government hospitals offer laparoscopy.
precautions: If fever or wound infection, seek care

symptoms: not a disease – guidance for safe use
benefits: eco-friendly, cost-effective, reusable for 10 years
guidance: Menstrual cups are safe if properly cleaned. Boil before first use and after each cycle. Wash with mild soap and water between changes. Change every 8-12 hours. If TSS symptoms (fever, rash), remove immediately. Do not use if IUD strings are long (risk of dislodgment).
precautions: Clean with boiling water between cycles
If fever or rash, remove and seek care

symptoms: rash, redness, itching, or burning in the vulvar/perineal area
may be due to fragrance, dyes, or prolonged pad use
guidance: Change pads frequently (every 4-6 hours). Use unscented, hypoallergenic pads. Wash with plain water and pat dry. Apply barrier cream (zinc oxide) or hydrocortisone. If persistent, switch to cotton pads or menstrual cups.

category: Iron Deficiency Anemia due to Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
symptoms: fatigue, weakness, pale skin, dizziness, shortness of breath, palpitations, cold hands, brittle nails, pica (craving ice/dirt)
guidance: Treat with oral iron supplements (ferrous sulfate) and folic acid. Dietary: leafy greens, jaggery, meat, and vitamin C for absorption. If anemia is severe, IV iron or blood transfusion. Control menstrual bleeding to prevent recurrence.
precautions: Avoid tea/coffee within 1 hour of iron
If heavy periods persist, treat the cause

category: Combined OCP and Risk of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
symptoms: higher with obesity, smoking, age >35, family history
guidance: Screening before prescribing OCPs: BP, BMI, smoking, and family history. If risk factors, use progestin-only methods. If on OCPs and develop leg pain, swelling, or chest pain – seek emergency.
precautions: If family history of DVT, avoid
Know warning signs (leg swelling, chest pain)

category: OCP Use in Women with Migraine with Aura
symptoms: women with migraine with aura are at increased stroke risk on combined OCPs
also risk if >35 with any migraine
guidance: Combined OCPs are contraindicated in women with migraine with aura. Use progestin-only pills, IUDs, or implant. If already on OCP, consider switching. Stroke risk is real.
precautions: If aura develops on OCP, stop

symptoms: used to evaluate ovaries, uterus, endometrium, and adnexa
guidance: Common indications: pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, fibroids, cysts, infertility. Transvaginal gives better resolution. Timing: best done in follicular phase for ovarian evaluation (days 5-10).
precautions: If pain during scan, may indicate pathology

symptoms: better visualization of endometrium, ovaries, and myometrium
used for early pregnancy, ectopic, bleeding, and IUD localization
guidance: TVS is safe, even in pregnancy. Empty bladder before scan. Comfortable but may be slightly uncomfortable. Provides high-resolution images. Essential for evaluating endometrial thickness.

symptoms: elevated in ovarian cancer, but also in endometriosis, pregnancy, or infection
not a screening test for average-risk women
guidance: Used in high-risk women (BRCA carriers, strong family history) or to monitor ovarian cancer treatment. Not recommended for general screening due to low specificity. If elevated, do transvaginal ultrasound.

symptoms: not a disease – procedure to destroy endometrial lining
used for menorrhagia in women who have completed family
guidance: Outpatient procedure. Good success rate (80-90%). Failure may need hysterectomy. Not for women desiring pregnancy. Also not for women with endometriosis (pain not resolved).
precautions: May still need contraception (tubal if permanent)

symptoms: not a disease – surgical removal of fibroids
guidance: Myomectomy is preferred for women desiring future pregnancy. It can be performed via laparoscopy, hysteroscopy (submucous), or open. Recovery 2-6 weeks. Risk of recurrence (up to 50%).

symptoms: not a disease – surgical removal of uterus
indications: fibroids, adenomyosis, endometriosis, cancer, prolapse, heavy bleeding
guidance: Hysterectomy is a major surgery. Types: total (removes cervix) or subtotal. Routes: abdominal, laparoscopic, vaginal. Recovery 4-6 weeks. Preoperative counseling: permanent infertility, possible ovarian failure if ovaries removed, and pelvic floor implications.

symptoms: not a disease – surgical removal of ovary/fallopian tube
for ovarian cysts, cancer risk reduction, or ectopic pregnancy
guidance: Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) causes surgical menopause if premenopausal. Hormone replacement is needed. Used in BRCA carriers to reduce cancer risk. Laparoscopic approach is common.

symptoms: available free in government hospitals under family planning
guidance: Tubal ligation is 99% effective. It does not affect hormones or menstruation. It is irreversible (though reversal is possible but not guaranteed). Counseling is essential. Done laparoscopically or postpartum.
precautions: Permanent – ensure no future pregnancy desire
Risk of ectopic pregnancy if failure

category: Reversible Contraception Options (OCP, Implant, Injectable, IUD)
symptoms: not a disease – guidance on reversible methods
combined OCP, progestin-only pill, implant, injectable (DMPA), copper IUD, hormonal IUD
guidance: Choice depends on age, risk factors, and preferences. OCPs regulate periods. DMPA causes amenorrhea. IUDs have different bleeding patterns. All are highly effective. Free at government family planning clinics.
IUD insertion is done in the clinic. May have pain (cramping) and spotting. Advise NSAIDs before the procedure. Check threads after next period. Ultrasound for confirmation if needed.
precautions: If pain or fever, seek care

guidance: IUD removal is simple. Usually done at any time. Slight cramping. New IUD can be inserted immediately. If strings not visible, ultrasound guidance may be needed.

category: Depo-Provera (DMPA) Injection – Side Effects on Menstruation
symptoms: often after 6-12 months, many become amenorrheic
guidance: DMPA is highly effective. Menstrual changes are common; reassure that it is not harmful. If bleeding is excessive, rule out other causes. Calcium and Vitamin D are important (BMD effect).
Irregular bleeding is the most common reason for removal. Reassure that bleeding is not harmful. If bleeding is unacceptable, consider add-on NSAIDs or OCPs. If persists, removal.

category: Menstrual Cycle Tracking – Apps and Diaries
symptoms: tracks period dates, flow, symptoms, ovulation
helps in fertility, PMS, and irregular cycles
guidance: Use a diary or app (e.g., Flo, Clue, Ovia). Track: start date, end date, flow, pain, mood, and any symptoms. Useful for doctor visits and identifying menstrual disorders. Also helpful for avoiding pregnancy or conceiving.
precautions: Do not rely solely for contraception

category: Basal Body Temperature (BBT) Tracking for Ovulation
symptoms: not a disease – fertility awareness method
guidance: Measure temperature daily at waking (before any activity). A sustained rise of 0.2-0.5°C indicates ovulation. Useful for fertility planning. It is not a predictor (confirms after ovulation).

symptoms: not a disease – test for LH surge
detects LH surge 24-48 hours before ovulation
helps in timing intercourse for pregnancy
guidance: Test daily from day 10 of cycle (or as per cycle length). Positive LH surge is the best predictor. Use with BBT to confirm ovulation. Helpful in fertility treatment.

symptoms: not a disease – tracking cervical mucus changes
changes from dry to wet, stretchy (egg-white) around ovulation
guidance: Observe mucus consistency daily. Egg-white (stretchy, slippery) indicates peak fertility. Dry = no fertility. Useful for natural family planning. Accurate when taught properly.
precautions: Use with other signs for accuracy

symptoms: provided feeds are frequent, day and night
guidance: Lactational amenorrhea is a natural contraceptive method (LAM) if: exclusive breastfeeding, <6 months, and amenorrhea. It suppresses ovulation. When periods return, fertility returns.
precautions: If no period after 6 months, pregnancy test if sexually active
Hormonal contraception may be used while breastfeeding

guidance: Non-breastfeeding: return around 6-12 weeks. Breastfeeding: may be 6-12 months. First periods may be heavy or irregular. Ensure adequate iron. Use contraception if not planning pregnancy.
precautions: If prolonged or excessively heavy, see doctor

symptoms: menstrual migraines, hot flashes, mood changes
guidance: Perimenopause is the transition (usually age 40-55). Bleeding changes are normal but must be investigated if heavy or prolonged. Rule out endometrial hyperplasia. Hormonal therapy (progestins, OCPs) can help manage symptoms.
precautions: Any very heavy bleeding needs evaluation
Do not assume all changes are menopause
